entities.summary:
Perceived oscillating motion of orbiting bodies relative to each other, libration is a fundamental concept in astronomy. In ancient Greece, Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310-230 BCE) first proposed a heliocentric model of the solar system, where Earth and other planets orbited the Sun, and their apparent wobble, or libration, was due to the Sun's motion. This idea was later refined by Copernicus (1473-1543 CE) and further developed by Johannes Kepler (1571-1630 CE), who discovered the three laws of planetary motion. The concept of libration has had a lasting impact on our understanding of the universe, shaping the development of modern astronomy and our understanding of the cosmos.

The actual events surrounding libration's significance began with the early Greek philosophers who first proposed the concept of a Sun-centered universe. This idea was further developed by Copernicus who presented his heliocentric model in 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' (1543). The Copernican heliocentric model was later refined by Kepler who discovered the three laws of planetary motion. These laws were first presented in his 'Astronomia Nova' (1609).

The legacy of libration can be seen in the development of modern astronomy. The concept of a Sun-centered universe laid the foundation for later discoveries and has had a lasting impact on our understanding of the universe. The discovery of the laws of planetary motion by Kepler further refined our understanding of the solar system and paved the way for later astronomers to make groundbreaking discoveries.

As Kepler wrote, 'The more I see of the universe, the more I am convinced of its harmonious design.'
